And not only was *it not asked for publicly, but the fact that it was procured was neveir made public, either by the registration of the deed or in any other way. Can the hon. minister point to a newspaper in Kent county that announced the fact that the government had purchased the sawdust wharf for $5,000? Not a newspaper in Kent county was made acquainted with the fact -not even one citizen was informed, beyond those interested in its procurement. Outside the perpetrators of the fraud, nobody was permitted to know the facts. Is there one hon. member who will stand in his place and say that Murray meant to suggest in that telegram that the very advertisement of the fact that the government had procured the wharf from him was a matter ' important to Leblanc '? Surely there is not one. If further testimony was needed, we have it from Mr. Murray himself. And that testimony is absolutely inconsistent with the theory of the minister, and it is on Mr. Murray that he depended again. When Mr. Murray was asked about the telegram, what was his first answer? The first was an absolute denial that he had sent a telegram to the Minister of Public Works or any officer of the department. How does the minister square the much-vaunted credibility of Mr. Murray with the fact that, in answer to question after question covering a third of a page of evidence, he persistently and emphatically denied that he had sent the telegram, and stuck to it until the telegram was produced before his face? He denies and again denies; the telegram is produced. The next question is: What do you mean by saying in the telegram that the purchase of that wharf was ' important to Leblanc '? What was his answer? I submit to the members of this House that if Mr. Murray had meant to say in that telegram that it was ' important to Leblanc ' for legitimate purpose, in the first place, he would not have denied sending the telegram, and, in the second place, he would have had in his mind at once the purpose for which the telegram was sent, and would at once have answered that it was ' important to Leblanc 5 from the public point of view that it should be known that the purchase was made. But Mr. MEIGHEN.
what was his answer? I think it is at page 66 of the evidence, but, at any rate, his answer was: I cannot tell you what those words mean. Here he was faced with his telegram stating that the procurement of this wharf by the government, and of $5,000 by himself, was ' important ' to the Liberal candidate, yet he tells the hon. member (Mr. Crocket), in answer to his question, that he has no reason to give for and no meaning to attach to the words ' important to Leblanc.' How does the minister square this with his theory? It is absolutely impossible. And it is just as impossible for him to square the reputation and honour of his own department, and of the head of that department, with the sending of that telegram by Mr. Murray. I make the assertion that, if that telegram stood alone surrounded by the explanation given of it by Mr. Murray, it would be conclusive proof of every assertion made by the hon. member for York. And the Minister of Public Works, in his laboured defence of his position, deigned to take some three or four minutes to refer to that telegram. Sir, if that telegram had not been sent, I venture to say he would have had more courage in addressing the House this afternoon. That telegram cannot be concealed, the signature to it can never be denied, and the existence of that telegram marks the exact position in which the minister stands in relation to this whole transaction.
Now, what is the next thing that occurs? Mr. Murray procures the $5,000. He got that money, I think, between the 12th and 15th of October, 1908-at any rate, in the first half of that month. He gets the cheque cashed, and he is careful to cash it in $5 and $10 notes. Now, why did he cash it in $5 and $10 notes? Is that the usual way in which $5,000 cheques are cashed? But, in the first place: would a gentleman of the extensive business, that of Mr. Murray-so extensive that he professed he could not remember the transaction-be likely to cash a $5,000 cheque at all? The minister knows that that is absolute nonsense; that it is not the habit of business men in this country or any other country. A gentleman of extensive business, part owmer of a railway, would not cash in $5 and $10 notes, or any other notes, a cheque for $5,000. He would deposit that cheque with his banker, and, if he had debts to pay, he would cheque the money out like a business man. Why did not Mr. Murray do that? Because the cheques would tell the whole tale of the transaction. But the Minister of Public Works asks, why did not he deny that he got the cash in $5 and $10 bills?-nobody -was there to make known the facts. But Mr. Murray knew it would be marked oil the back of the cheque, and there would

be no possibility of denying it. But, to go on:	What did he do with this $5,000?
Took it home and gave it to his wife. Is it usual for a business man of the province of New Brunswick, receiving a cheque for $5,000, to draw the cash in $5 and $10 notes and take the money home and give it to his wife? Especially, is that usual just about fifteen days before a general election? The man who does it is one of the campaign managers of the Liberal party in Kent county, New Brunswick. But the mystery does not end there, and to call it a mystery would be a euphenism. He pays out $5,000, and he cannot tell any of the persons to whom he paid it except to another campaign manager of the Liberal party, and he does not know what on earth he paid him. Now, Mr. Speaker, have you, in the course of your business or public career, ever seen a transaction like that? Is there a precedent for anything of that sort in the history of honest dealing in this country? $2,000, he wont deny it was that, which he paid to Geo. W. Robertson, who saw the minister in the matter, and who later on accompanied Mr. Murray to Ottawa to see the minister in St. John, and who was a partner with him in managing the Liberal party in the county of Kent, paid him $2,000 in cash in payment of a debt, but he cannot tell what the debt was for or how much the debt was. But it does not end there. He knows nothing about all the rest of the debts which he paid with the other $3,000. But strange to say the only debt that up to that time had come to light as touching Mr. Murray, is the debt that he did not pay at all. He owed Mr. O'Leary a large sum of money, but he did not see fit. to turn in -any of this money to Mr. O'Leary. Perhaps the explanation, is that Mr. 0;Leary was not a joint manager of the Liberal party campaign fund in Kent Now, what is the next thing? The next thing that occurs after this deed is registered, is the public scandal, it becomes a matter of notoriety, it passes from mouth to mouth, that the old heap of sawdust has been purchased by the Dominion government shortly before the election for the colossal sum of $5,000. That comes to light just after the general election. A scandal ensues, as tlie minister practically admits, and that scandal proves that Mr. Carters judgment was sound when he decided that this deed should not be registered until after the general election was safely passed. The scandal ensues, the Minister of Public Works hears of it from the member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Leblanc), a gentleman of parts, and so far as we know, a gentleman of honour. The member for Kent, who, strange to say, knew nothing about this transaction, who had never represented to the Minister of Public Works that there was any earthly use for this heap of sawdust, goes to the Minister of Public Works and complains that it is a scandal to the honest community that the government should pay $5,000 for a wharf like that. Then the Minister of Public Works gets busy and he begins to write letters. He writes a letter to Mr. Stead and a letter to Mr. O'Leary, and in those letters he betrays those same symptoms of injured innocence that he manifested to the House this afternoon. And he proclaimed it as a great credit to himself that he wrote to Mr. O'Leary after the election was over and after the facts about this transaction had been disclosed.
A great credit to him when the notoriety of the scandal was rampant throughout Canada, and when nothing but this was possible for him to do in order to cover up the evidence of the job that has been committed. Now, Sir, the minister writes to Mr. O'Leary; Mr. O'Leary replies, just as one would expect him to reply. The minister writes to Mr. Stead, and here is something that is certainly worthy of attention ; the ingenuity with which the Minister of Public Works met this was something that should go down as of scientific importance, if for no utner cause. Now, Mr. Stead was in the witness box in December, and he swore that he did not see the Minister of Public Works about thi3 transaction from the time of his report on the 10th June, 1908, until the minister wrote him a letter on the 13th January, 1909. Now, the minister's letter was meant to convey the impression to those who read it that he had very recently been informed that Mr. Murray had purchased this wharf for a small sum of money, and had within a few days turned it over to the government for $5,000; he meant to convey'the impression to Mr. Stead that he had only just been informed of this, and was innocently waiting for information. No other meaning could be taken out of that letter of the 13th of January; the letter is in the Hansard, and I need not quote it again. Do you believe. Mr. Speaker, thajt these were the facts, that the minister had just been informed of it, and that he was for the first time apprising Mr. Stead of the position? The minister tried to convey the impression to the Public Accounts Committee that those were the facts. But those were not the facts. Worse than that, the minister actually endeavoured before the Public Accounts Committee to put into the mouth of Mr. Stead a statement which was not a fact, and which it is impossible to believe the minister did not know was not a fact. The minister himself was the gentleman with whom Mr. Stead consulted on the 26th December about this very transaction, 20 days before he wrote the letter. He meant to put into Mr. Stead's

mouth that he had never seen the'minister about the transaction at all between the 10th June and the 13th January, and Mr. Stead, after the words were put into his mouth, positively swore that he had never seen him about it. But when Mr. Stead was brought before the committee, and when he was compelled to produce his diary, he was compelled to admit that he had seen the minister about it, and had actually discussed this transaction with him on the 26th December. That is something the minister did not bring to the attention of the House. Not only that, but the minister told him he had better get out and produce some evidence, discover some facts, in order if possible to support the transaction. That is what took place on the 26th December, so - far as the evidence shows. The evidence does not show that anything more was said; but it does show that the matter was discussed between these two gentlemen, and Mr. Stead also stated that the minister told him he would write him a' letter about it, and that Mr. Stead expected the very letter that he received on the 13th January, 1909. And how does the minister square that with the contents of the letter itself; and why did the minister not frankly state that, he had discussed this matter with him on the 26th December, if the minister was as innocent of the whole transaction as he would have this House believe?
Now, Mr. Speaker, put all these circumstances together, and what is the only conclusion? That is for the members of this House to decide. It is what the minister has not answered, it is what no hon. member on the other side of the House has attempted to answer. What is the significance of the chain of circumstances-a chain of circumstances on half the extent of which more than one man in this country has been hanged? The hon. member for Carleton and the minister himself tried to wipe out the shame of this transaction by bolstering up the value of this wharf. Whether this wharf is worth $i or $5,000,000 is of very little consequence in so far as the guilt of the minister and the shame of his department are concerned. If this wharf is worth $10,000,000 to-day, what does it signify and how does that affect the direct and plain responsibility of the minister for the whole fraud connected with this transaction? How does that impair the chain of circumstances that all along show the cognizance of the department of the deliberate attempt that has been made to filch out of the treasury of this country money for the carrying on of elections in the province of New Brunswick? If that wharf was sold at $700 and then, a few days after, sold for $5,000 I venture to say that to the unprejudiced electors of this country there will be no explanation for

it except the explanation that I hope this House will accept.
On the matter of valuation I do not propose to say very much. On the question of valuation, in order, if possible, to divert public attention from the enormity of the crime, they dwelt long. Valua-* tion ! In every trial or legal procedure in this country at which questions come up that involve expert testimony, expert testimony and information can be procured. If it were a matter of valuation you could procure valuations for any purpose whatsoever and every lawyer in this House knows it. But, Sir, the fact that stares the people of this country in the face is that a wharf that had laid idle for fifteen or twenty years, worthless and unused, in a village of 700 people, constantly declining, in numbers, is sold for $500 in 1905 to one Frank Ingersoll, who pays $50 down, then rues his bargain and forfeits his $50 because he believes that the wharf is not worth the other $450. The minister had it in his power, if he disbelieves Mr. O'Leary in that regard, to call Frank Ingersoll, but he did not do it. The wharf remains from that time on until May, 1908, when Mr. Thomas Murray suddenly buys it after visiting the Minister of Public Works, for $700, and in thei course of eight days has virtually completed a transaction by which he sells it to the government for $5,000. The sale of that wharf for $700 on the 4th of May, if it were worth what the minister and his friends claim, is only accounted for by one hypothesis, and that is the absolute insanity of Mr. O'Leary. Nobody says for a moment that Mr. 0'Learj>
is a dupe. He was not away down in the southern states, or in South America, or in India, he was living right there on tne ground, the largest property owner in the town, admitted by every person to be shrewd, capable business man. He sells that wharf for $700 on the 4th of Mav and the government are actually forced to make this country believe, if possible, in support of their position, that when he sold it is was actually worth from $5,000 to $15,000. That is what the government are faced with. But, that is not all. AVho else has given evidence as to the value of this property?
I submit to the minister and to you, Mr Speaker, that the assessor of Richibucto is a man who ought to know what this property is worth. It is on record that the assessor of Richibucto, after Mr. O'Leary had sold the wharf, refused Mr. O'Leary's request to reduce the assessment by reason of the wharf being sold and gave as his reason that the wharf was of no value whatever, and that, consequently its alienation did not detract from the value of the whole property. If the minister disbelieves Mr. O'Leary in that regard, why did he not call the assessor? The minister

did not call the assessor, and he did not call Ingersoll; he is obliged to call those who have intimate connection with his own department and in whom the obligation to be on good terms with the department heavily rests. The assessor is therefore on record. But what more is on record? What is the criterion of t'he value of property anywhere? It is, first, what shrewd business men will buy it for; it is, secondly, what other property sells for in the neighbourhood, and I submit to this House and the minister that every record of sales in Richibucto absolutely gives the lie to the position of the Minister of Public Works. Case after case was put on record by the hon. member for York. I do not need to go over them again, but we have it on record that this wharf for which the government paid $5,000 was sold for from seven to twenty times what it was actually worth. Against this the minister can call till Doomsday those who have [DOT]contracts from the government, those who are making money out of his department to give evidence, but the people of the country have too much common sense to listen to any evidence of that sort after the evidence of actual facts.
When is the time coming in this country, when is the time coming in this House, when hon. gentlemen opposite will venture to throw off the garments^ oi party and vote what they actually believe to be correct and true with respect to a resolution before the House. When is the time coming when we can rely on hon. members of this House to vote against transactions that are exposed as this one has been in the light of day and whose true character must be admitted by every member of this House? If the minister says:	Make a charge-for what purpose
make a charge? In order that there may be an investigation? I tell him that this has already been investigated and that the minister has been there to defend himself. He was there throughout the whole inquiry. What more does he want in the way of investigation? The evidence is there. Now, I aver that while this class of transaction does not stand alone, this is one of the worst that has ever been brought to light against this government. It is true that this is only a breath from that atmosphere of political depravity that envelopes this government and supplies the only nourishment upon which it can subsist but this debate is surely not without a purpose, and I hope it will have this result that the minister will never again proclaim in this House or on the hustings that he carried the province of New Brunswick and thereby vindicated his own character and the administration of the department over which he presides.

Mr. Speaker, this matter has been so fully debated that I do
not intend to occupy the time of the House for more than a few moments. The amount involved is not a large one, but the question at issue is not without importance, because I think we may learn from the methods disclosed in this transaction some of those which perhaps are applied to transactions of greater amount. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works did not seem to be so much at ease as usual when he was undertaking to defend this transaction this afternoon, and I do not wonder at that. He made some rather curious suggestions in the course of his speech. For example, he argued strenuously-and I am inclined to think that we ought to accept his word-that if any telegram with regard to campaign funds had been sent by Mr. Murray, it would have been sent to him and not to Mr. Valiquette. My hon. friend was ready to give his assurance to the House in that regard, and I am, inclined to think that, according to the well understood usages of parliament, my hon. friend from York and my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie should have accepted this statement.
I do not propose to quote any evidence, but to consider certain facts seriously disputed. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has based his defence, if you can call it a defence, upon certain theories as to the value of this property derived from the evidence of certain witnesses given before the Committee on Public Accounts. I prefer to take events and transactions when there was no controversy at all about the value of this property, and when men acted upon what they believed to be its value. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie has put in a very few words what I desire to say in that Tegard. Here was a property purchased for $400 in 1902, sold for $500 in 1905, just three years before this transaction, sold to a man who put up $50 and preferred to lose that sum rather than carry out his bargain. The owner of the property, Mr. O'Leary, according to the judgment of the Minister of Public Works, and according to the judgment of the hon. member for Carleton, is as shrewd and capable a business man as is to be found in the province of New Brunswick. That man, after having had this property on his hands for years, after having paid $400 for it and having vainly tried to sell it for $500, sold it in the month of May, 1908, for $700, and thought that in doing so he made a very good bargain. In addition to that, when he went to the assessor of the town afterwards, and endeavoured to get the taxes on his property reduced by reason of the fact that he had parted with this property, he was not able to get one cent taken off his taxation, for the reason that the assessors considered the property of so

trifling a value that they could not conscientiously reduce the value of his remaining property on the municipal records.
Is there any dispute about these statements?

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question? In the province of New Brunswick real estate and personal property are assessed at exactly the same ratio, and the personal property that Mr. O'Leary got in the shape of money would take the place of his real estate, so that he would not be entitled to any reduction

Will any hon. gentleman in this House be good enough to tell me what answer I ought to give to the hon. gentleman's 'question'? Let us go on a little further. There had been some negotiations between Mr. Murray, the purchaser of this property, and Mr. O'Leary, the owner of the property, previous to the occasion on which this property was actually purchased. There may be some dispute between these two gentlemen as to whether or not in the first instance there was a negotation as to a purchase of the whole property. I have listened very attentively to this debate. I have endeavoured by examining the evidence itself as the various speakers went along, to follow up this matter, so that I could come to a correct conclusion about it; and so far as the various controversies are concerned that have arisen between Mr. Murray and Mr. O'Leary with respect to matters of fact, I venture to think that any 'hon. gentleman in this House who gives an intelligent consideration to that evidence, cannot fail to accept the statements of Mr. O'Leary and reject those of Mr. Murray. If my hon. friend from Carleton should have evidence of that kind presented to him when he comes to accept one of those judgeships which have been alluded to this afternoon,
I have sufficient confidence in his judicial fairness to believe that without one single moment of hesitation he would accept the statement of Mr. O'Leary and reject that of Mr. Murray. I say further than that, that if my hon. friend from Carleton, sitting as a judge upon the bench, had evidence of this kind presented to him upon the motion of my hon. friend from York, he would not stop to reserve judgment, but would give judgment on the spot in favour of my hon. friend from York upon the evidence adduced. I am glad to see that my hon. friend from Carleton smiles assent to that.
Almost any man would smile at a statement like that.

I do not see why my hon. friend should smile at the idea of his possessing judicial fairness. Let us look a Mr. R. L. BORDEN
little further into this matter. According to the testimony of Mr. Murray, the only purchase spoken of in the first instance wras the purchase of a right to place a sewer through this property. It is established that Mr. Murray went to Ottawa afterwards. It is established again, although the evidence was extracted with great difficulty, that he saw the Minister of Public Works. Is Mr. Murray so much in the habit of coming to Ottawa and visiting the Minister of Public Works that he cannot remember what took place or what induced him to come on any particular occasion? Will any hon. gentleman have the hardihood to rise in his place and say that he can credit the testimony of a man who came to Ottawa on an occasion of that kind, saw the Minister of Public Works, and when interrogated on the witness stand, was absolutely unable to give any explanation of his visit except the one that has been suggested by my hon. friend from York? Well, he went back to New Brunswick, and what occurred then? He wanted to purchase this property outright. There is no dispute about that; he admits it, and O'Leary stated it. He had suddenly,for some reason, acquired the idea that it would be greatly to his advantage to become possessed of this property as its owner.
He did become possessed of this property for the sum of $700. Mr. O'Leary was not only willing but absolutely delighted to get rid of the property at that price. Now, Mr. O'Leary had held this property for a number of years, he had carried on business in that town for a number of years, and according to all the evidence given he is a shrewd business man. But in parting with this property for $700, Mr. O'Leary must have been absolutely bereft of his reason if the property were worth anything like $5,000. Then, some further things happened which are not without significance. There had been a proposal in the previous March, that a certain municipal wharf should be acquired by the government and a report had been" made favouring the acquisition of that wharf. The resident engineer of the Department, of Public Works was sent to make and he did make a new report, and changing his view of the situation for some reason which he did not very satisfactorily explain, he arrived at the conclusion that it would be desirable to purchase this property and he advised the purchase of it for $5,000. If his report is to be trusted he regarded that as a very reasonable price Indeed. Now, in the course of his examination, not at first but during his subsequent examination he was compelled to admit that at the time he signed that report he knew that that property had been conveyed by Mr. O'Leary, by means of a deed of conveyance which expressed upon its face that the purchase price of this pro-

perty was not more than the sum of $1,000; and this purchase had taken place barely one month before the time he reported that $5,000 would be a fair and reasonable price for that property.
Only sixteen days before.

Sixteen days. I did not know it was so close as that;_ I was certainly not exaggerating the peculiar feature of the situation in that regard. Now, I would like to know from the Minister of Public Works whether he would have put through that purchase if he had known that that property had sold for $700 in the previous May. The Minister of Public Works did not give us any explanation in that regard. He did write a letter on the 13th of January, 1909, and I am bound to say that that letter has fully served the purpose for which it seems to have been written-it has been quoted in this House. That letter expresses the disapprobation of the Minister of Public Works of the course this engineer pursued in not reporting that that property had been sold for not more than $1,000 just sixteen days before he made his report. To show how deep was the disapprobation of the Minister of Public Works of this action of his engineer, I am informed that he not only _gave_ him the statutory increase of $100 in his salary, but he gave him a special bonus increase to the extent of $200 besides. I venture to say that having been taught a lesson, such as that, this engineer will never sin in the' same way again. I do not- know of more condign punishment that can be visited upon a man for negligence of that, kind than to give him the usual statutory increase and give him a special increase of $200 besides. Still, matters did not proceed rapidly enough, and later, on the 13th of September, Mr. Murray sent a telegram to Mr. Valliquette, whom he designated as chief engineer of the Department of Public Works, and Mr. Valliquette was entreated by the terms of that telegram to hasten this transaction for the reason that it would be very important to my _ hon. friend (Mr. Leblanc) who is the sitting member for the county of Kent. I do not know whether my bon. friend from Kent agrees that this transaction was important to him; I have rather understood that he dissents from the view of Mr. Murray. At all events the telegram was so effective that the Minister of Public Works, on the 24th of September, made a report to council, an order in council was passed, the transaction went through and the money was paid to Mr. Murray about the 10th of October. Mr. Murray describes himself as a man of large business transactions. He is part owner of a railway and his transactions with Mr. Robertson
and other gentlemen are so extensive, and they have become so confused in his mind that he is unable to recollect the details of a single transaction. And in order that there may be absolutely no question in regard to this he received the whole $5,000 in $5 and $10 bills. I want hon. gentlemen to realize what this amount of bills would mean. Assuming that the sum of money was equally divided between $5 bills and $10 bills, Mr. Murray went home with no less than 750 bank notes in his pocket, and he handed them over to his wife. Then, he proceeded to deal with that money according to his usual business methods, and in the first place he paid to Mr. Robertson, the gentleman who had accompanied him on his visit to Ottawa, the sum of $2,000 in partial payment, or in entire payment, ot in over-payment, or in some kind of payment, of a" debt, the nature of which or the amount of which he is absolutely unable_ to describe. He had taken the precaution in the first instance to carry home the 750 bank bills and after that he paid the $2,000 out. Is there any hon. gentlemen in this House so simple minded as to place credence in a story of that_ kind. Is it not taxing our credulity a little too much to ask us to believe that this was an ordinary plain business transaction as the Minister of Public Works would have us believe. Why, the story is absolutely incredible upon its face. Sir, this is an absolutely undefended case. I will not take up the. time of the House further than to say that every credit is to be given to my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) for exposing this transaction. ,1 tor mv part con-gradulate him upon his action in this case. I may say that when he brought this resolution and submitted it to me before presenting it to the House, I said to him: its terms are preitty strong; can you make them good; do not go any further than that which you are able to maintain by reference to the evidence upon the floor of parliament. And my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) said to me: I can make it good. And Sir, at this moment I have only one criticism of his resolution and that is that I do not think he made it strong enough.

For the development of the live stock industry, $52,000.
Mr. .1. D. REID. Give us some explanation about that,

By way of explanation, I have to say that we have been continuing the same work as was done in years past in regard to this branch. It has been under the guidance of Dr. Rutherford, who is not only director veterinary general, but also live stock commissioner. He has as assistant, Mr. Spencer, who is in more immediate charge of this work. The work consists in aiding the development of the live stock interests of the country by the encouragement of local live stock associations, and the distribution of information among those and among men interested in the live stock work. In this connection we have been supplying judges to fairs or exhibitions, and assisting those exhibitions by supplying speakers to address them, and give illustrations and information. We have also a staff of men who have been attending institutes where live stock interests are being discussed. We have also sent out a great number of bulletins. It was under this branch that what is known as the sheep bulletin was sent

out last year, and just recently a bulletin, or report of the Swine Commission was sent out. We have also undertaken work in connection with the breeders of pure bred cattle. The breeders of pure bred cattle, dairy cattle especially, have asked that steps should be taken to make what is called an advance registry of dairy cows, and for this purpose they wish to have authoritative tests. We have appointed inspectors to go about and supervise these tests, and we give the necessary service.
Who are the commissioners?

The first inspectors are Mr. Drummond, Mr. Clements, Mr. Mason, and Mr. McNish. There are four of them now. When the work first commepced a few years ago, it was thought that on& man would be able to attend to it, but there has been such a demand that as time went on we have had to add to the number, until now there are four engaged, and occasionally we have to employ temporary men for outlying parts which these four inspectors could not conveniently, or economically reach. This work has been demanded by the breeders of pure bred cattle, especially, and it is one which I think of importance for the improvement of these breeds. It has met with great favour among the people interested, and also among those who wish to buy sires for breeding stock and improving their own herds. We have also made some money grants to certain fairs in the west and in the east. The grant to the Maritime Stock Breeders' exhibition at Amherst, and to some fairs in the western provinces, has come out of this grant. We have been doing a little work in the direction of the developing of the sheep industry. We have tried to give instruction and information in regard to that. In that connection, we have been arranging and managing the sales of sheep by auction in different parts of the country. This is a general resume of the position, but I shall be glad to answer any question.

If a diseased animal is slaughtered by order of the department on a report from, one of the departmental veterinary inspectors the owner is reimbursed for the loss of the animal. But, the government department will not take the diagnosis of a duly qualified veterinary surgeon who is not in the service of the department. If such a practitioner is engaged by the farmer, the government will not take his certificate that a horse is suffering from glanders, for instance, but the farmer runs the risk of having his whole stock infected while he waits for the departmental inspector, or else if he slaughters his horse he will not get any compensation. It does seem to me that that is unjust and^ unreasonable. I do not see why the certificate of a duly qualified veterinary surgeon should not be taken as well as that oi a government official, who has just 1 2461
the same qualifications. Several farmers have complained to me in regard to this matter, and I think the law ought to be changed.

On account of the spread of glanders in the country, some years ago, I asked parliament for a handsome appropriation to try and eradicate the disease, and in order to meet with any success I found it necessary to pay compensation. The hon. gentleman from North Toronto and others pointed out the danger of raids on the public treasury in such cases, and I assured the House that we would pay compensation only upon the certificate and responsibility of officers of the department. The ordinary veterinary surgeons are the employees of the owners who are asking for. compensation, and other countries as well as our own have suffered in the payment of compensation for slaughtered animals by reason of that fact. It is a very simple thing for the owner of a horse to isolate the animal if he is affected with glanders, and if he telegraphs he will get a veterinary surgeon within a day or two at the outside, generally the next day. If other horses have been in close contact with the diseased animal, then, probably the whole stable of horses will have to be slaughtered, and it would be very dangerous to undertake that responsibilty on the certificate of any but an officer of the departs ment. We do that for the safety of the community at large, and it is on that plea and that plea only, that we are entitled to pay compensation. I do not know any country in the wnrld that pays compensation upon the certificate of a private practitioner. I think it would be unwise and unsafe and contrary to the pledge I gave to parliament when this money w-as placed at my disposal. I am glad to say that while in the first year we spent over $150,000,'-the year before last -we spent only about $40,000, and in the year just past about $70,000, and I hope that in a short time we shall get the disease so thoroughly under control that it will not be a menace to the horses of the country.

difficulty could be got over. collusion, it would be sympathy and a desire to please the neighbour and employer. I understand there is no work on the diseases of poultry. There is very little information.
