It would need some further experimental work or investigation to determine all these different diseases. I believe that if a man were appointed for this work, the different provincial institutions and the different breeders could furnish enough specimens to keep him employed.

I guess so. However, it is an interesting question that has been raised and it might be worth while to set a man to this particular kind of work. 1 confess I was not aware of what my hon. friend says that the diseases of poultry were so obscure and that so little was known about them. I believe some other governments have been doing some work along that line and I should have supposed that tire diseases of poultry were fairly well known. But I will make inquiry into that, and if we can see our way clear to make an investigation with respect to the poultry, we might do so. It is a matter of great importance to the country and might be worth while.

The reason I have mentioned the matter was that the discussion seemed to be going in that direction. In the United States they have a man, Dr. Morse, who has done some good work. I believe that the Veterinary General sitting beside you will bear me out when I say that little is known of the diseases of poultry. My authority for that is Professor Graham, who has made quite a study of the matter.

I think the question raised by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Russell) is an important question, and the Minister of Agriculture would be doing a good thing if he would appoint an expert to work constantly along these lines. There is no doubt in the world that thousands of dollars worth of poultry is lost through disease, the causes of which are not known. Take for instance the raising of turkeys. I know that in many parts of the country, farmers will not try to raise them because of the diseases that occur. Perhaps when they are a couple of months old, they show signs of disease, and in many cases die. And the farmers have
no means of knowing what causes their death. I think if would be a very wise thing to have a competent man to work for a year or two or for a greater length of time if necessary.

I would like to call the minister's attention to a suggestion I will be bold enough to make. We have in Kingston as in Montreal, and in other centres, universities. Those universities have on their staffs some very able men. Take McGill University, for instance, and Queen's University, than which there is no greater or better on the continent of America. We have in those universities, pathological experts. Now, would it not be well to make use of the laboratories of those universities and the expert knowledge we have there. These men, so far as I have been able to observe, throw their whole heart into their work and would devote 25 hours of the day, if there were 25 hours iu a day, to their work. I think it would be a good idea not only to make use of tlie universities in this regard, in the way of making tests and researches, but also for the veterinary inspectors and veterinary surgeons in the immediate vicinity of those universities to come in contact with those men, and have conversations with them on this matter. In tjiat way you will be more likely to get results than by all the efforts of the department, no matter how sincere and how well directed they may be. It seems to me that that could be done with great advantage to the country in general.

I may say we have done that to a certain extent. We have asked professors of universities to undertake microscopical investigations. Very often we have found that they were so busy with their own work that they could not undertake it in a reasonable time and we have had to do it ourselves. But sometimes they have assisted us. I remember Dr. Gordon Bell of Winnipeg, doing some work and we have had Dr. Adami of McGill, while Professor Todd is now doing work for us. I also remember some years ago a professor of Queens university doing work for us, I forget his name at the moment.
Dr. Connell, I presume.
Yes.
You could not have had a better man.

Of course all these gentlemen have their own work in connection with investigations and teaching in the university, and not infrequently they would be' very glad to take up work of the kind mentioned if they had the time. We have two other pathologists besides the two in Ottawa, one in British Columbia, and

the ether in Lethbridge, Alta., investigating special diseases. So we are fairly well equipped. Still there is more to be done.

The minister has referred to the new regulations under which veterinary surgeons must give their whole time to the service. Can he give the date of that regulation?
Experimental farms, $110,000
I see that the Minister of Agriculture has an item of the same nature in the supplementary estimates. The one discussion would do on both. We do not want to sit too late to-night.
Yes, we might as well pass this.

It has always been in existence applying to cases where we pay an annual salary, as is done in the case of the majority of these veterinaries. It has come more into practice since the change of the head of the branch. Dr. McEachern when head of the branch only gave a portion of his time and a good many of the men under him did the same. When Dr. Rutherford was appointed he gave his whole time to the work, and we are working that idea in.
Is the regulation in force now?

Not absolutely. Some of the old appointees are still on. In Montreal we have the same officers who were managing the inspection of cattle and horses for export. They practise in Montreal privately, and receive so much a year from us. There are Dr. Baker, the second Dr. McEachern and Dr. Sugden.
If they engaged in practice, would they be disqualified? Would the minister dismiss them?

I should consider it very objectionable. I would prefer to deal with each case according to circumstances. If I found a salaried man not giving his whole time to the department, I should be disposed to warn him. Where we give a salary we expect the man's whole time.
And do I understand that the salaries are $1,000 and $1,200 for veterinaries in the west?
Some do work as low as that. The highest, I think, receive $2,000.
If a veterinary in the west were given only $100 a month he would have to be allowed to practice and -earn extra money. Because $1,000 or $2,000 is no salary for a veterinary surgeon in the west.

We give them enough to keep them busy.
Arts, agriculture and statistics-census and statistics, $50,000.
Some hon. members asked me to hold this over for some information. A question was asked as to the regulations in regard to census taking I have that information.
Carried.
That is what I was going to suggest. Then we could have the discussion on the supplementaries.

I have three items in the supplementaries. Perhaps we could take them up.
Department of Agriculture-
To provide for two clerkships in second division, subdivision A.. $3,200 To provide for seven clerkships in second division, subdivision B, 4 at $1,200; 1 at $1,125; 2 at $800..	7,525
Contingencies-Further amount required	 2,o00

There are two things in which extra assistance is required. One is the archives and the other the experimental farms. In the archives we have a mass of documents which are not catalogued and, therefore, not properly available to the public. Many are interested in these documents. For instance, lawyers are constantly coming to get information concerning cases which turn upon old documents. I have asked for further assistance in order to proceed more vigorously and rapidly with the cataloguing, so as to make these documents more available to the public.
Will these officers pass the examination and come under the Civil Service rules?

Yes. In the experimental farms, I have to make some slight reorganization. Dr. Saunders has asked to be relieved of certain detail and routine work with which he has concerned himself personally, but which ought not to be imposed upon the head of such an important system. I have to throw that work on other officers, and so I ask for two assistants on that part of the work at the farms
Arts, agriculture and statistics-experimental farms-further amount reauired $20,000. '

I have already explained the increase in the number of experimental farms and the need of a larger sum for their administration. I now hope to be able to establish more of them than I thought would be possible when the main estimates were prepared, and, therefore, I am asking for this supplementary vote.
Will the minister explain what methods he intends to pursue in the selection of these experimental stations?

I wish to place them where they will serve a large area-to place each in a piece of country that seems to he as near a large area of adjoining country as possible. Then I wish to place each of them in a conspicuous place. And I wish to place each of them at a point easily accessible. These are the main objects.
How is the minister going to acquire that information? By his own observation?

Of course, so far as the area of the country is concerned, we have a fair record of that in the various departments, and the people themselves know pretty well the places that are characteristic of a large area. This last summer I had an experienced officer going about and examining the best sites. I am constantly deluged with offers of farms, and when I receive such an offer, if it seems to me to be in a suitable locality, I send a person to examine it.

Has the minister had any inquiry from the Carman district in Manitoba? It is one of the best railway centres in that western country, and very suitable for an experimental farm station. There are three lines of railway, the Great Northern, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern, and another line is projected.
I do not remember that we have had an application from Carman. I would like the farms to be spread over the province, not to have them in too close proximity.

I presume the new farms will be under the direction of the managers of the experimental farm we have now; if so, it would be convenient to have them situated not too far apart. Now, if you place a farm down near Boissevain, your manager could come down there and inspect it and go back the same night.
Has the minister arrived at a decision with regard to a farm in the interior of British Columbia?
We still have that matter under consideration.

I would suggest to the minister that east of the city of Winnipeg we have a large area of very fine land, but there has been so far no effort made by the government to direct settlers into that part of the country. It strikes me it would be a splendid thing to put one of these stations in some place east of Winnipeg,! and I would urge the minister to do that.
I have had some repre-: sentations to that effect, and they will receive consideration.
How many stations does he propose starting this year?
I have in mind- at least half a dozen new ones. I have instructed an officer to examine suitable sites in Manitoba.
Are you going to establish any more in Ontario this year?
I hardly think so, this year. I have had representations from New Ontario, and possibly there will be one there.

My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is not present tonight, and I would suggest that we allow item 421 to stand, so that when it is taken up again any hon. member may discuss anything in relation to experimental farms.

I will consent to that on condition that we take it up again not later than to-morrow, as I have to be away early next week.
Grant to Charlottetown exhibition for 1910, $10,000.

This is a new vote. We have been giving $50,000 for exhibitions in each of the provinces, but we have never done that in Prince Edward Island. Some -years ago when the Dominion exhibition wa3 at Halifax they asked us to give them $10,000. This year the Dominion exhibition is in St. John, and Prince Edward Island has asked for the same consideration, and we do not think it unfair that they should have $10,000 in one year and' $10,000 another year.
Quarantine-steamers to replace ' Argus J and ' Challenger '-revote, $39,000.
I suppose this is in regard to. the boat being built for Halifax! harbour? Would the minister say what' position that boat is in?
She will be completed and delivered in the course of the coming summer.	-

It seems to me strange that this boat should have to be built in Dartmouth, England, in view of the fact that we are about to build .a navy in Canada. It does seem strange that we cannot construct a boat 80 feet long by 19 feet wide and 8 feet hold. Has no effort been made by the government to construct this boat in Canada? We hear a great deal' about the construction of Dreadnoughts and torpedo boats and all other kinds of boats, but we have not been able to construct a small steamer for the quarantine service.

The explanation is simple. We asked for public tenders and we, received tenders from a large number ofi firms in Great Britain and Canada. The; tender for the boat which we accepted was; $22,000 odd, and the next lowest in Canada was $32,000, or over $10,000 difference, and we did not see our way to paying that extra amount of money.
This is $39,000.
There are two boats.
Where is the other vessel being built?
We are just advertising for tenders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are a number of small votes in civil government in the Supplementary Estimates for the year 1911 which are of a purely routine character, and I would suggest that we call them and if there is any objection they may be allowed to stand.
Civil government - Department of Militia and Defence-to provide for one clerkship in second division, subdivision B, $1,200.
This is all Greek to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These all come under the operation of the Civil' Service Act, except the case of one lady whose name is mentioned.
Are they additions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In some cases they are.
Department of Secretary of State-to provide for one statutory increase omitted from tile main estimates, $50.
How did the omission take place?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The various departments, in making up their statements, sometimes omit something. They are very correct in the main, but being only human, they are not absolutely perfect.
This seems to be in-i creasing the number of clerks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In several instances.1 there are increases.
No decreases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think there, are any; it is a growing time.
Department of the Interior-salaries and contingencies, $12,000.

I would like to ask the Finance Minister if it is not the custom of the government to provide for gratuities for the benefit of the families of Civil Servants who die in the service.
Mr CROSBY

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is an established practice, that at one time was confined within a small circle, but it is now broader, providing that an allowance equivalent to two months' salary of the deceased official is paid to the widow or family.

The reason I ask it is that the death occurred recently of Mr. John Flesher, who was formerly land agent in my town, but, who, during the last five or six years, had been residing in Winnipeg. He died a month ago and I do not see any provision in the estimates for a gratuity, to his family.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would not be necessary. There are some gratuities in connection with the Northwest Mounted Police, and the Department of Militia and Defence which are voted in accordance with the', Act, but the provision for a gratuity of a two months' salary is a general provision and is to be found in the Civil Service Act. If my hon. friend will drop nre a note giving the name of the official and his position, I will see that whatever is customary is extended to his family.
Office of the Auditor General-to provide for four clerkships in the third division, subdivision B, $2,000.
Only $2,000 for four new clerkships?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The nevv appointees; will come in at small salaries. The object of this is that I have been asking the; Auditor General to undertake a service which he has not hitherto performed.
That is all right; I was surprised at the low amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They begin at small salaries. The object is to take some of the higher men and assign them to the duty of inspecting the Minister of Finance, -to see that the gold is all to be found in the place where it is supposed to be.

I do not believe very strongly in commencing men in any kind of responsible clerkships at a very low salary. If we require a clerk at all we should give him a salary that would be in keeping with the position he undertakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These are young men who begin at the foot of the ladder. Their duties are not very responsible.
What is the statin tory increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: $50 in each case.
What will their salaries be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: $500 and $50 per year increase.
What will their responsibility be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They will be junior clerks.
The Civil Service Act provides for this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.
They will not have the responsibility of handling money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; the Auditor General handles no money whatever. He simply keeps watch upon the other fellows.
I understood the minister t-o say that all these clerks come under the Civil Service Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, unless a name is specially mentioned here.
And they are appointed by the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
A commissioner has nothing to do with whether a clerk is required or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The department would call upon the commission to furnish the number required, and then an examination is held, and the high men get the place.
Assay Office, Vancouver, $18,000.
Has the government any assay office?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is one at Vancouver.
Oh, yes, I know, but you should establish one in eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have^ as a matter of fact, two assay officers in the city of Ottawa.
Yes, but they are not established to do business for the public, and they charge high fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: One part of this vote is to employ an extra assayer.

I am not objecting to the vote, but I draw the attention of the minister to the fact that the government has no assay office in eastern Canada, and it seems to me that in the interest c>f mining development, and discovery, they should establish one here. The thousands of prospectors who are out every year require to have their samples assayed so that they may get a return in a few days because the only way of telling what is in the sample is to have it assayed. But the ordinary prospector cannot pay $2 for each assay, as is charged in the government office at Ottawa. One party sent me three or four samples and asked me to have them
assayed here, but I was told I could not get returns for two weeks perhaps, and that the charge was $2 for each test for a mineral in the one sample. I wrote back to the gentleman who sent me the samples telling him the facts that there was no use going to such expense as that. We hear a great deal about minerals in northern Ontario and Quebec, and I do not believe there is any part of Canada in which there are so many minerals. It would be but a trifling expense to the country to establish an assay office in eastern Canada, where the assay could be done at actual cost, and be reliable. In the case of some of these private assayers the test is not reliable, and I would urge strongly upon the government to take action in the direction in which I have indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The assay office in connection with the Mines Branch here does assaying for the general public, and a month or two ago I authorized the director to employ another assayer. I do not think the fees charged are very high. It must be remembered that there are a great many private assayers established throughout the country, and if the government is going to do free assaying it would simply drive these men out of business. I doubt very much if that would be fair play. We are carrying on the work of assaying primarily in the interest of the department, and every specimen collected in that connection has to undergo a very exact test. That is the work of the Department, to carry on that technical work so that our mining engineers anil geologists can get up the reports properly. But aside from that we do assaying for the general public, and for that we charge fees. I do not think it would be right for us to charge less than a private assayer. If we did, we would put many of them out of business at once.

That seems to be a strange position for the minister to take, that he should charge the same fees as private assayers, no matter whether they are extravagant or not. That means that he is in a combine. The provincial assay office at Belleville takes no account of the charges of private assayers, but has a regular scale of charges, which are supposed merely to cover the cost. I think the charge for a gold assay is 50 cents. The government assay office here gives no encouragement to the prospector who goes out to discover minerals. If he sends a lot of samples to Ottawa to be assayed, he is told that he will have to wait until the office gets through with the samples of the Geological Survey; then they will attend to his; and perhaps it is a month before he can get any Teport as to whether his samples are good or not. If the govern-' 1 ment have an'assay office, they should not

pay any attention to what assayers charge elsewhere. They should charge the pubiic or the prospector simply the actual cost.
Senate-to provide for making good tlie full sessional indemnity of members of the Senate-days lost through absence caused by i'lness during the present session-and $2,500 tc pay the sessional indemnity of the Honourable James Domville for the session of 1906, absent ithrough illness-notwithstanding anything in chapter 10 of the Revised Statutes, an Act respecting the Senate and House of Commons, $11,180.
Is this the first time this question has been raised?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is the first time. The hon. gentleman referred to was on his way to Ottawa when he met with an accident. He was not able to reach Ottawa, and technically was not entitled to the indemnity.
House of Commons-to provide for making good the full sessional indemnity of members of the House of Commons-days lost through absence caused by illness or public business during the present session-notwithstanding anything in chapter 10 of the Revised Statutes, an Act respecting the Senate end House of Commons, $11,820.

I would like to know what that means? There are a great many of us who stay here and diligently do our work; but I understand that that means that if we do not stay here we are to be' paid as if we do. I must protest against! that. Many of us make great sacrifices of money to stay here and attend to our public duties. As 1 understand this item, it is to provide that gentlemen who are not here, but who leave the burden of the affairs of the country to those of us who do stay, are to be paid the same as if they were here. If it means that, I protest against it, though I am not going to divide the House upon it. I am not speaking of one side of the House more than the other;
I am speaking generally of the principle involved. Those gentlemen who do not stay here, go away beeanse it pays them to go, because they make money by going away. They ought not to be paid by the people when they are being remunerated in some other respect by staying away. That is the protest I make. It is not that I want to deprive any hon. member of his full indemnity if he earns it, but I do say that if it pays him better to leave his place in this House of Commons and go away to attend to other affairs, and I think we must take it for granted that it does pa,y him better or he would not go, he ought not to ask this country to pay him for being in this House when he is not here. I think that the Act passed in 1903 or 1905 ought to apply.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not di sagree to any extent with my hon. friend (Mr. Lan- Mr SEXSMITH.
caster), but I think he has misconceived the intention of this vote. He is certainly not correct when he says that the man who goes away and devotes himself to his private affairs is to receive more consideration than the man who attends to his duties in this House. This clause would only affect members who conscientiously sign a declaration that they have been absent through illness. The law provides that if a man is ill in Ottawa, it shall not count against him, but if he happens to be sick a few miles away, it would count against him. One must draw the line somewhere. The Act says that those who are ill in Ottawa are entitled to receive the full indemnity. The change which this vote makes for the present session is that a member who is ill at some other place in Canada shall be entitled to receive the indemnity. :

A man might be ill and yet be able to earn money. I think the test should be whether he is attending t-o the affairs of the country or whether he is attending to his own private affairs. A man might be ill, and yet be able to attend to his business. If he swears that he was too ill to work at all it would be alright and he would have our full sympathy, but if he is not too ill to attend to his' own private affairs, I think the Act should apply. The work we do in the House of Commons is not by any means the most healthy work. I myself am pretty hard, and pretty tough, but I have made myself ill by_ working here late at nights, and am suffering from the strain, and from not having enough sleep. If tire declaration is to be that he is so ill that he cannot attend to any business, I would be inclined to agree, but the argument of the Minister of Finance that a man has only to be away from home because he does not feel first-rate holds good, he might be attending to his medical practice or to his store or to his farm, he might not be so ill that he could not attend to his own private affairs.
I do not think that by merely saying that he is in bad health he should draw his indemnity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should think that an hon. member who is able to attend to his private affairs would not make a declaration that he is absent through illness. When it comes to a matter affecting the personal honour and affairs of a member,
I think each one of us must be content to leave the other to make the declaration and to make it in all good faith. Let me give an illustration. An hon. gentleman who usually sits on the opposition side has been ill, and has been obliged to leave his parliamentary duties, and go south. I refer to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). He is ill and

away from Ottawa, but it cannot be said that he is attending to his business. He has left his business in Montreal, and has been obliged to go south. I do not mention him particularly, because there are others. This would entitle that hon. gentleman to the full indemnity, as full as he would have received if he had been ill in the city of Ottawa. If one is ill in the city of Ottawa, and is able to remain here, he suffers no reduction, but if his physician says he had better go south, it does seem a hardship that he should lose his indemnity while another member in Ottawa gets it. It is difficult to draw any absolute line in these things. In preparing the estimates we try to take a generous view of all cases.
A member might be ill and might not be able to get properly treated in Ottawa, and he might have to go to some other locality where he could get the proper treatment.

I ao not like this manner of doing it. We are repealing by an estimate, or practically repealing, an Act of parliament. I think it would have been better to have brought in an Act amending the Act of parliament. An Act of parliament is a different thing from an estimate. Supposing the public did not agree -with this change, supposing the people of the country did not think it was the right way to do it, then I suppose there would be no suggestion of bringing it up next year. Then some member might be ill next year, and suffer very unjustly. I think the proper way to do would be to take the responsibility of bringing in an Act to amend the Act. I do not think this is the proper way to do it at all.

I see this item is for an odd amount. I would like to know how the minister arrived at the amount stated here, because it was not generally known on this side of the House that anything of this kind was in contemplation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it was known on that side of the House. When this matter was proposed, I do not- mind telling my hon. friend, that I had conferences with members on that side of the House, not unusual conferences, and I gave instructions to the accountant to ascertain what amount would be drawn by the various members in question, if they did not suffer this disability.
Suppose some members fall ill between now and px'orogation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afra'd they will have to.wait until next year then. That was the way it was done. The accountant ascertained what amount lion, gentlemen in each case had drawn, and what was the
balance they would be entitled to, and the sum placed here is sufficient to cover all cases of that kind.
I may say that I had a conference with the Minister of Finance with respect to certain members who have been sick during the sess;on. And the minister has made up the estimates on this basis.

We members on this side of the House have no knowledge whatever of anything of this kind. And I, as a member of this House, object to any private or semi-private arrangement of this kind being made for individual members of the House from which the members generally are excluded.
Included?
Excluded.
Nobody is excluded.

There are many members of this House who suffer disabilities from their attendance here much more serious than the penalties of some of those who have been away 'during this session. I can see no reason why there should be a special vote of this kind passed at the end of each session for persons who have the ear of the government or who have been alert enough to lay a special case before the government whereby they shall obtain from the treasury of the country payment for no service rendered. If it is desirable to follow this plan, then the Act should be changed so as to make it applicable to all members equally. I for one, if I had been prevented by illness from putting in attendance here, would feel it derogatory to my independence as a member of this House to make a claim on the government for the time I had lost. I do not think that I should be penalized for time I might lose by illness while at home, yet another hon. member who has not attended at all during the session should be paid his full indemnity. Such a member has not incurred any expense or sacrificed any time in coming here. I was greatly surprised at the end of last session at the indemnities voted by this House. While I am on my feet, I would call the attention of the government to a feature of the indemnity which bears with especial hardship on those who come, as I do, from the remote parts of the west. The point I refer to is the calling of this House together in November. This means an adjournment in December, for about four weeks, which compels us to travel
3,000	miles each way across the continent to go home and back travelling entirely at our own expense and with the loss of a week on the road each way. There is also the adjournment at Easter for a -week

when we must either go back and return to Ottawa again at our own expense or stay here in idleness and lose the time. For all this we get no compensation. Yet we are asked, after being at all that expense and all that sacrifice of time, to vote indemnity for members who have not served the public at all. I do not think that is right. I quite understand why it passes year after year without protest, for it is a very delicate thing, when the names of persons who are to have the benefit of this suggested vote are mentioned in the House, for any of their colleagues to rise in their places and object. But I think it is time that some person did object, and I object strongly to the singling out of certain persons for special favours making them the beneficiaries of an Act which does not apply automatically to all members of this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This appropriation does apply automatically to every member of the House under the conditions.
Mr. ,T. D. TAYLOR. Then, why did we not know about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It can only be because the hon. member (Mr. .T. Li. Taylor) has not read it; it tells its own story. When he speaks of this item extending to one member and not to another he is mistaken. The words of this Act would apply to any hon. member who has been ill away from the city of Ottawa during the session. If any hon. member has been absent from Ottawa and that absence has been due to illness, he lias a right to claim the benefit of this item. If there is not enough money in it, more must be provided by a later vote. There is no distinction between one member and another. It is hardly correct to speak of any member in this case 'filing a claim.' No one has filed a claim. The whip of the other side had a consultation with me and named the persons whom he thought should be dealt with in this way.

And that is not filing a claim.
Air FIELDING I should hardly call
it so. Some of the names mentioned were mentioned without the knowledge of the parties concerned. But we tried to remember the names on both sides of gentlemen who might be affected. I would like to have it clearly understood that there is no possible discrimination in the matter. Whether we are wise in making this appropriation as. for the time being, an amendment of the Act is a fair question of debate. I think there is much to be said in favour of adhering rigidly to the Act. But that is a beautiful theory, and so often we are not able to live up to these theories. Every session some peculiar case arises, circum-Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
stances in reference to a member or a member's family need to be taken into account. We cannot deal with these things on lines of cold-blooded logic, but must take into the account some of the claims of human sympathy. We -are weak in these respects and we fall. It has been so in the past, and I expect that it will be so again.
If the hon. minister is going to fall again-I do not disparage his statement, I think I have as much charity as he has-I want him to fall generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He does.
And I want him to pass an Act of parliament to justify his fall.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is an Act of parliament.

Yes, but it is an Act of parliament brought in at the end of the session. And it is needless to disguise the fact that, as the hon. member for New Westminster (Air. J. D. Taylor) says, there is a discrimination. We do not know, at the beginning of a session, that this Act is going to be put through. The matter is at the "mercy of the government, An order in council has to be passed to put in that estimate; it must go through the cabinet like a public work or a post office. The thing is in the gift of the government, and is not the right of a member of parliament when parliament opens. The member concerned is at the mercy of the government as to whether they will do him this favour or not. That is what I protest against. If the hon. minister believes what he says- and no doubt he does-and if he believes in the wisdom of what he says, then why can he not amend the law and leave the matter to the operation of the law? That would be the manly, the proper, the businesslike way to do. Alake it so that everybody will know at the beginning of the session what is to be done, and so that the matter will not depend upon communication between the whips on either side and the government as to the members who should be served in these matters. It ought to be the right of a member of this House and the right of all equally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is exactly the case. It is his right.

No, because the matter does not come before parliament at all until the government first takes action. I do not believe in this being done by order in council. I think I make that plain, I agree with my hon. friend from New Westminster that this more or less strikes at the independence of parliament. Some of us do not like to go and ask the government to make a special estimate and over-ride the Act of parliament for our benefit. We

must not be so toucliy about criticising these things. The general law should be amended so that it will apply automatically to all within the description of the law. The thing should be made a matter of right for the member or for his heirs if he should happen to die. I protest against this thing being done by order in council, as it is when it comes in the supplementary estimates. I think the Minister of Finance should carry out what he defends, and do it as a business man by amending an Act of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only reason why this has come from the government is that it is a money matter. I do not think that any hon. member on either side of the House availing himself of this amendment to the law, comes under an obligation to the government. If he draws a sessional indemnity under the general Act he has to get that by the government of Canada coming here and proposing that that Act be adopted. This is an amendment to the statute. When this estimate is passed into law it becomes for the time being, as respects these people, an amendment to the statute; and if any hon. member who avails himself of the benefit of that comes under an obligation to the government, then he is equally under an obligation to the government when he draws his salary, or allowance under a general Act. In both cases he gets it upon the initiation of the government, but that does not involve any obligation to the government.

Surely the hon. gentleman sees the difference. In the one case, every session, at the dying hours of the session, we should have to have an estimate brought in by the government saying that for this session we shall be paid so much indemnity. On the other hand the statute is there and fixes the indemnity. The hon. gentleman surely does not mean that that statute can be repealed and that we should come in at the end of every session and have supplementary estimates brought down saying that we shall have so much indemnity.

I do not think after all there is much difference between this proposition, and what we have been in the habit of doing for many years. I have often thought that the statute itself was wrong in insisting that a man, in order to be relieved, had to live in Ottawa, or within ten miles of Ottawa. If he lived beyond that then he had to lose a part of his indemnity. During the present session I have been ill in Ottawa, and been prevented from attending the House. I do not lose the eight or ten days I have been ill, but had I been ill at home I certainly would have. I do not understand why there should be a distinction between a
man living in Ottawa, and a man living a hundred miles from Ottawa as regards illness. I think this proposition is more in accordance with justice thaij the Act we have upon the statute-book. I know one hon. member, whose name I will not mention, who was absent nearly two months on public business, and I do not think it is fair that he should be called upon to lose his indemnity when he is obliged to be absent. I have no hesitation in supporting the proposition. It has been an old custom ever since I have been in parliament, over twenty years, that if a member dies during the session the full amount of the indemnity which has not been paid to him shall be paid to his legal representatives. If the head of the family is taken away by death, I think it is a proper thing to see that the widow gets the indemnity. We have done that all the time, both in regard to senators, and to members of the House of Commons.

I agree with the remarks of my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson). I wish to bring up one case that occurred a number of years ago where I always felt that the member was treated unfairly, I refer to Mr. Livingstone, who was then member for North Waterloo. He broke his leg when not in Ottawa, and the House refused to give him his indemnity. I brought the matter up at the time, although he was a member on the opposition side of the House.

I have no objection to the passing of this item. But I agree with my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) that as this is a question that comes up every year, why not have a statute that will cover it, and have the thing settled? Suppose a man who lives in the far east, or in the far west, on account of illness in his family, has to remain at home two or three weeks, is that not just as serious as if he was sick at home? I believe that the fifteen days grace that is allowed by statute to members who have to come here for four or five months in the year, is not enough, I believe we should have a longer grace. I think it would be fair to say that we should have at least four or five days in the month, because it is impossible for one living as far east as I do to leave here on Friday night and get back before the following Tuesday night. I believe that a committee of this House should take the matter up and see if it cannot be regulated and a statute formulated that would cover it so that eyery man would know what he has to expect.
I would like to know whether this item provides for the full sessional indemnity to new members who have not been here and who have been elected since the session opened?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A member elected dur* ing the session and obliged to be away byi illness would be entitled to draw as much indemnity as he could have drawn if he had remained in Ottawa.
Before he was sworn in a member of the House?

Yes, from the date of his return, I think, would be the proper way to treat it, and if he were prevente.d, by illness from being sworn in he would be still entitled to his indemnity. That is the way I would interpret this item, but, he would not be entitled to a full indemnity, because he was not a member for the full session.

I say this is a most improper proceeding and a most invidious ease. I do not think that there is any gentleman who was so ill that he could not come up and take the oath or take his seat in the House. It only adds force to what' I said before as to the impropriety of these proceedings. If an hon. member gets elected as a member of this Flouse, pays no attention to his election, goes away for months, comes back here and draws his full indemnity it is a most improper proceeding and one we should not countem ance. Votes of this kind should be closely scrutinized every time and not allowed to go through without discussion. What proportion of this vote is to go for days lost by absence on public business during the present session? There is no public business appertaining to the duties of a member as such which calls for his absence from the House, and I do not think that any member should be paid his indemnity as a member of this House for public business otherwise performed. We have suffered in the House of Commons this year, we have been delayed far beyond the time when we might have been expected to return to our homes because of the absence of members of the government. It seems to be rubbing it into us to ask us, after keeping us here, to vote the full sessional indemnity to ministers who have been away on business which did not necessarily call for their absence from the House, and on business which might have been performed by other per-* sons quite as well as by these ministers.
1 do not think it is a proper principle. This indemnity is paid to members of parliament for their services in parliament. If they do not perform these services, but accept other employment, whether under the Crown or otherwise, I think it is an improper principle to pay them their full indemnity. How much of this sum is to pay for days of absence caused by public business?

If any member of the government has been away attending tg Mr. J. D. TAYLOE.
other public business, it is the hon. member's contention that he might have remained in the House attending to his duties here and that some person else might have performed the duties that the member of the government performed during his absence. In that ease, is it not true that whoever else might have been employed in place of the member of the government would have been paid for his services. In that case what difference would it make?
It. might have been performed-by a civil servant drawing his salary.

The hon. gentleman did not say that a civil servant could have performed the duties and probably he could not have. The hon. gentleman spoke of the case of a man who had not taken the oath or taken his seat. I cannot see that thah makes any difference to a man's equitable right at all. There is only one case this session that I remember of to which the remarks of the hon. gentleman would apply. I understand that when, that hon. gentle-i man went away from the city he had to bet carried to the train upon a stretcher. Surely the hon. gentleman would not desire that a man should be carried on a stretcher to the House of Commons to take the oath in order to be entitled to his indemnity?
Did he take the oath?
I understand he did not.
My opinion is that a man is not a member of this House until he signs the roll and takes the oath.

The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) has argued that, a man outside of this House should be paid as if he were in the House. I quite agree with my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor). A man is employed here just as he is employed by anybody else. The people employ that man to come here, and do the public business. If he is not here doing that business he should not be paid as if he were. The hon. member for South Grey would not employ .some one in his absence if he were ill, and pay both of them. He would not employ two men to do the work of one, and pay both. There may be reasons, as was stated by the hon. Minister of Finance, which would cause us to take a charitable view of some of these cases, but I would say to the hon. member for South Grey that surely he is not going to argue that there should be a statute saying one thing, and the sweet will of a cabinet saying another at the end of every session in regard to whether a man is to be paid who is not here. As a matter of principle the statute should speak

for itself. If it is not fair, amend it, but let the people of the country know what the rights of a member are, and do not let us have this at the end of every session.
It is now a quarter past twelve, and perhaps it would be better to let this item stand.
Carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I want to say to the hon. member that I cannot tell him how much money would be paid under these words. The words were taken from a previous vote. I am inclined to think that perhaps no money would be paid under the terms of these words, but I will not say that definitely. I only know of one case to which they might refer. L may say to my hon. friend that the hon. gentleman referred to has made no application whatever I am surprised at the opposition that is manifested to this vote, and I desire that it shall stand.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business is to be taken to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The House will be moved into Committee of Supply, and I believe there will be discussion on that motion. In Supply the estimates of the Minister of Interior will be taken.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.18 a.m., Friday.
Feiday, April 22, 1910.
